```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(metamicrobiomeR)
```

The 1.x functions are still in the package, with the same arguments and output, so you do not have to move. This
vignette is for when you want the newer importers, engines and diagnostics.

## Results that differ from version 1.2 and the 2019 paper

* **Mixed-model p-values.** In version 1.2, `taxa.compare()` and `pathway.compare()` computed the p-values of linear
  mixed models as `1.96 * pnorm(-|z|)` in place of `2 * pnorm(-|z|)`, so they were about 2% too small (for example
  0.0088 in place of 0.0089 in Table 3 of the 2019 paper). Version 2.0 corrects this, so rerunning an old script gives
  slightly larger p-values. GAMLSS models and cross-sectional linear models are not affected, and no conclusion of the
  2019 paper changes.
* **Pooling.** `meta.taxa()` now pools a taxon only when at least two studies have an estimate, and it warns when one
  study holds most of the weight or a standard error is implausibly small. See `vignette("notes-earlier-results")` for
  the Coprococcus example.
* The full list is in the package NEWS (`news(package = "metamicrobiomeR")`).

## Running old scripts

Old scripts run unchanged. The worked example of the 1.2 vignette gives the same tables and identical plots in version
2.0, apart from the differences listed above. One thing to check: version 1.x installed the `gdata` package, and its
vignette used `gdata::drop.levels()` to remove unused factor levels. Version 2.0 no longer needs `gdata`, so a script that
calls it stops with "there is no package called 'gdata'". Either install it once with `install.packages("gdata")`, or
replace the call with base R:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# version 1.x vignette
taxa.meansdn.rm$bf <- gdata::drop.levels(taxa.meansdn.rm$bf, reorder = FALSE)
# base R, same result
taxa.meansdn.rm$bf <- droplevels(taxa.meansdn.rm$bf)
```

## Function map

| 1.x | Modern workflow |
|---|---|
| `read.multi()`, QIIME 1 tables | `legacy_to_study()`, `as_study()`, `read_dada2()`, `read_qiime2()`, `read_metaphlan()`, `read_biom_study()` |
| `taxa.filter()` | filters inside `fit_study()` (`min_prevalence`, `min_mean`) |
| `taxa.compare(propmed.rel = "gamlss")` | `fit_study(engine = "bezi_gamlss", n_cycles = 20)` gives the same estimates |
| `taxa.compare(propmed.rel = "lm", transform = "asin.sqrt")` | `fit_study(engine = "lm_asin")` |
| `pathway.compare()` | `read_function_table()` then `fit_study()` |
| `alpha.compare()` | `fit_alpha()` |
| `meta.taxa()` | `pool_effects(method = "DL", test = "z", adjust_by = c("part", "term"))` |
| `metatab.show()`, `meta.niceplot()` | `plot_forest()` |
| `microbiomeage()`, `taxa.mean.plot()`, `taxa.meansdn()`, `taxcomtab.show()` | no modern equivalent, keep using these |

## Where the defaults differ

* **Unassigned lineages**, such as `...f__lachnospiraceae.other`, are left out of the modern models.
* **Pooling** uses REML with the ad hoc Hartung-Knapp test, in place of DerSimonian-Laird with a normal test.
* **False discovery rate** is adjusted within a rank, in place of across all ranks.
* **Iterations:** see `?fit_study` for the current default of the GAMLSS engine.
* **Engine with repeated samples:** `fit_study()` uses `bezi_glmmtmb` when the model has a subject random intercept and
  glmmTMB is installed. Set `engine = "bezi_gamlss"` to match 1.x.

## Presence as well as abundance

The zero-inflated beta model of version 1.x reports only the abundance part: how the relative abundance changes in
samples where a taxon is present. A taxon that differs mainly in how many people carry it can therefore look unchanged.
In a meta-analysis of 15 public colorectal cancer studies, Fusobacterium was not significant with this model (adjusted p
0.37), while the mixed-model engine found it present in more people with cancer (adjusted p 0.0016). To report both parts,
add a prevalence formula:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit_study(study, ~ group, engine = "bezi_glmmtmb", prevalence = ~ group)
```

The result then has rows with `part = "abundance"` and `part = "prevalence"`, and `pool_effects()` pools each part
separately. A negative prevalence effect means fewer zeros, so the taxon is present in more samples.

## Converting a table

`legacy_to_study()` takes a table with samples in rows and taxa in columns named in the QIIME 1 style.

```{r convert}
data(taxtab6)
study <- legacy_to_study(as.data.frame(taxtab6), list(id = "Bangladesh", feature_type = "otu", subject = "personid"))
study
```

These tables hold relative abundances only, so the count-based engine `"zibb_glmmtmb"` cannot be used on them.
